title: Britain's codebreaking computer Colossus was kept secret for 30 years

cover.alt: A wartime black-and-white photo of a Colossus Mark 2: tall racks of valves and switches, with two Wrens at its slanted control panel and paper-tape frame.

body: **Colossus** helped codebreakers at Bletchley Park read the Lorenz cipher, used for messages between the German High Command and its armies. Designed by Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers, it used thousands of valves to compare and count bits from a looped paper tape, and it is regarded as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer. Ten were working by the end of the war in Europe. Afterwards almost all were broken into parts too small to reveal their purpose, and the machines stayed secret until the mid-1970s, so for decades they were left out of the history of computing.

slides.question: Colossus read its message tape with light sensors. How many characters per second did it read in normal use?
slides.explanation: 5,000 a second. In tests the tape ran at 9,700 a second before it fell apart. Five processors working in parallel gave an effective 25,000 a second.

slides.heading: Higher or lower: valves in early computers
slides.note: Sceptics doubted that even one or two thousand valves could work together reliably.
slides.explanation: Colossus did its job with far fewer valves than ENIAC's 17,468.

slides.text: That was a terrible mistake. I was instructed to destroy all the records, which I did. I took all the drawings and the plans and all the information about Colossus on paper and put it in the boiler fire. And saw it burn.
slides.attribution: Tommy Flowers, on the order to destroy the documents

slides.heading: Beaten by a laptop
slides.text: In 2007 the rebuilt Colossus raced radio amateurs to crack Lorenz messages. Joachim Schüth won easily with code he wrote himself: his 1.4 GHz laptop found the settings of all 12 wheels in under a minute, reading text 240 times faster than Colossus.

slides.question: Which German cipher was Colossus built to attack?
slides.explanation: Not Enigma, which was attacked with Alan Turing's electromechanical Bombes. Colossus worked on the Lorenz teleprinter cipher that the British called Tunny.
